title: Valencia: charity is metaphorical form only; faith and charity are distinct virtues
source_text: VI. Quibus consona sunt quae observat Gregorius de Valentia, eandem fidei distinctionem in formatam & informem explicans. Theologi, inquit, affirmant fidem a charitate tanquam a forma perfici. Nec tamen sentiunt, quod charitas proprie sit forma fidei, aut essentialis, ut Anima dicitur forma hominis, aut accidentalis & extrinseca, ut albedo corporis. Hoc enim falsum esse ex eo perspicuum est, quod charitas & fides sunt duae virtutes specie distinctae, quae duas diversas potentias perficiunt. Solum igitur volunt Theologi, charitatem, quoniam perfectionem aliquam addit fidei, metaphorice dici posse formam ipsius, secundum analogiam videlicet ad formam proprie dictam, quae suo modo subjectum perficit. Tom. 3. in Summam Thomae, Disput. 1. quaest. 4. puncto 5.
pass_a_gloss: Consonant with these are the things Gregory of Valencia observes, explaining the same distinction of faith into formed and unformed. Theologians, he says, affirm that faith is perfected by charity as by a form. Yet they do not think that charity is properly the form of faith, either essential, as the Soul is called the form of a human being, or accidental and extrinsic, as the whiteness of a body. For that this is false is clear from this, that charity and faith are two virtues distinct in species, which perfect two diverse powers. Therefore the Theologians only will that charity, since it adds some perfection to faith, can metaphorically be called its form, namely according to analogy to a form properly so called, which in its own way perfects the subject. Tom. 3 on the Summa of Thomas, Disputation 1, question 4, point 5.
pass_b_english: Gregory of Valencia agrees: theologians say charity perfects faith as a form, yet not as an essential or even accidental proper form — faith and charity are species-distinct virtues perfecting different powers.
Charity may only metaphorically be called faith's form by analogy to a proper form that perfects its subject.
